name: Site enhancement oil (Synthol)

card.summary: Oil injected straight into muscle to make it look bigger; case reports document embolism, granulomas, nerve damage and infection.
card.note: Medical literature documents serious complications including pulmonary oil embolism and stroke; no clinical trials exist.

quick.overview:
Site enhancement oil (SEO), best known by the brand name Synthol, is an oily liquid injected into muscle to increase its apparent size or alter its shape. It has been associated mainly with bodybuilders who use it on lagging or disproportionate muscles, a practice called fluffing [1].

The injected oil does not build muscle tissue; it sits in the muscle as a deposit. Medical case reports describe a range of complications, and the wiki found no clinical trials of its use.
quick.mechanism: Wikipedia reports a Synthol formulation of about 85% oil, 7.5% lidocaine and 7.5% alcohol, with sesame oil commonly used; some people instead inject poly(methyl methacrylate) or paraffin oil [1]. The material distends the muscle mechanically. A Sunday Times report cited in Wikipedia says injected muscle is not truly developed and may droop under gravity [1].
quick.risks: Reported complications include pulmonary embolism, nerve damage, infection, sclerosing lipogranuloma, stroke, oil-filled granulomas, cysts and ulcers, and allergic vasculitis from sesame oil; a 2011 case study reported multi-organ dysfunction in a user of multiple substances [1]. Wikipedia says synthol is not restricted and is sold online, while PMMA for muscle shaping is prohibited in the US [1].

lead: Site enhancement oil (SEO), best known by the brand-style name Synthol and also called santol, is oil injected directly into muscle to make it look bigger or to change its shape. Bodybuilders use it on muscles they want to appear fuller, such as biceps, triceps, deltoids and calves, a practice nicknamed 'fluffing'. [1][2]

The appeal is that the visual effect is immediate: the oil adds volume at the injection site rather than building muscle fibre, so a lagging or disproportionate muscle can look more developed on stage or in photos. A review of its use describes the enlargement as immediate and the product as acting like a temporary implant placed deep in the muscle. [3]

The medical literature on SEO consists of reviews and case reports, mostly from surgeons and endocrinologists who treat people after injection; no clinical trials of the practice exist. The reports describe scarring, fibrosis, oil-filled granulomas, deformity of the muscle, and in some cases raised blood calcium. [4][5][6][7]

chain: Oil is injected into a lagging muscle
Volume is added at the site immediately
Muscle looks fuller and more proportionate
angle.text: People inject site enhancement oil to change how a muscle looks straight away, filling out a small or lagging area to improve proportions. The volume comes from the oil rather than from new muscle tissue, and the shape can change as the oil spreads or the tissue reacts.

infobox: Synthol not restricted and sold online; PMMA for muscle shaping prohibited in the US per Wikipedia [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes SEO as oil injected into muscle to enlarge it or alter its shape. A 2009 review reports that Synthol typically contains about 85% oil (often medium-chain triglycerides), 7.5% lidocaine as a painkiller and 7.5% alcohol, and describes it as a temporary implant injected deep into the muscle. [1][3]

Other materials appear in the case literature: sesame oil has been identified in some mixtures, paraffin oil in Danish cases, and some people inject poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), a non-absorbable filler, to sculpt rather than merely enlarge muscle. [1][8] A Bulgarian surgical series grouped Synthol with vaseline and silicone as 'shell-less' non-absorbable fillers. [9]

Wikipedia says some bodybuilders, notably professionals, inject oil so that muscles look more developed where they are lacking or out of proportion, and that its sources describe the practice as common in the sport. [1] A Polish review lists the small muscle groups most often targeted as triceps, biceps, deltoids and calves. [3]
Case reports show use outside competition too: a 2021 report describes a woman who received Synthol for buttock augmentation. [10]

Reviews and case reports list nerve damage, oil embolism in the lungs, pulmonary artery occlusion, myocardial infarction, stroke and infection among serious complications, and describe deformed, unnaturally shaped muscles. [3] Wikipedia also cites sclerosing lipogranuloma, oil-filled cysts and ulcers, and a sesame-oil allergic vasculitis. [1]

A 2024 Danish review says injections can cause potentially lifelong problems in the musculoskeletal system, including scars, chronic wounds, pain, muscle deformity and loss of function. It names magnetic resonance imaging as the best way to map the condition and lists treatment as antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, compression and surgical revision where possible, adding that prevention is crucial. [4]

A 2024 plastic surgery case report describes a 45-year-old man with severe fibrosis and recurrent infections in the pectoral region after Synthol; surgical excision of the fibrotic tissue was performed. [5] A 2020 report and literature review on upper-arm injections concluded that the medical and sports communities should be aware of severe complications. [6]

A surgical series of eight patients, three of them with Synthol for muscle enlargement, found that oil-based fillers cannot be removed by minimally invasive techniques because of diffuse oleogranulomas, inflammation and fibrosis; surgery is followed by scars and often contour deformity, and the fillers can migrate to other areas. [9]

A study of 88 men who had injected paraffin or synthol oil into muscle about six years earlier found hypercalcemia in 34%, and kidney stones in 48% of the hypercalcemic men. Larger injected volume and injection of heated oil were among the risk factors, and the authors linked the effect to granuloma macrophages producing active vitamin D. [11]
Individual case reports from 2021 and 2025 also describe hypercalcemia after Synthol injections, one with granulomas in the lungs. [10][12]
Wikipedia states that Synthol is not restricted and that many brands are sold online, while the use of PMMA to shape muscles is prohibited in the United States. [1]

In T Nation threads the word appears mostly as an accusation or joke about unnaturally shaped arms or traps, for example a poster saying a physique is 'synthol, not photoshop', and another quipping that biceps will grow once a delivery of it arrives. [13][14] One poster in a 2021 confessions thread asked for 'a synthol protocol'; no instructions are documented here. [15]

No studies found testing site enhancement oil as a treatment. The existing literature consists of reviews, a surgical case series and case reports describing complications, including a cross-sectional study of 88 men with hypercalcemia after paraffin or synthol injections. [4][9][11]

timeline.event: Media reports on SEO use are cited in Wikipedia's article. [1]
Polish review of Synthol use in bodybuilding describes composition and complications. [3]
Study of 88 men reports hypercalcemia after paraffin or synthol injections. [11]
Danish review and a surgical case report describe lifelong musculoskeletal complications and fibrosis. [4][5]

lore.intro: In lifting forums Synthol is discussed as a visible marker of a muscle that looks injected rather than trained, and occasionally as something members say they might try. [13][15]

claims.claim: Injected oil makes a lagging muscle look bigger right away.
claims.believers: Posters note that visibly oversized triceps or traps are assumed to come from synthol, reflecting a shared belief that it works on appearance. [13][16]
claims.experts: Reviews agree the enlargement is immediate but describe the muscle as deformed and unnaturally shaped, with serious complications. [3]

claims.claim: Synthol is a shortcut to arm size that training does not provide.
claims.believers: A confessions-thread poster suggests it as an alternative to gaining weight to add inches to the arms. [15]
claims.experts: Published reports describe fibrosis, granulomas, hypercalcemia and surgery for removal; no trials of the practice exist. [4][9][11]
